Projects vs three tiers — you're right, that's not what the UI should be

The frontier sub-agent studied memory + frontend. Short answer: the engine supports your model; the product wiring conflates tiers with projects.

What you intended

  • Corporate / Professional / Personal = separate knowledge/memory bases (the "brain" / vectors) — not navigation tabs
  • Projects = main tabs you create — each with its own files, memory/guidance, and sessions (chats with orchestrator → leaders → workers)
  • Unlimited sessions per project as work grows

What the code actually does today

Backend — mostly correct at the engine level:

  • Three tiers exist as separate document repo roots (RepoScope in repo/paths.py: corporate/, companies/, users/)
  • project_id flows through orchestration, G1.5 leader reuse, threads, per-project file layout (users/<id>/projects/<project_id>)
  • Sessions correctly belong to projects and drive the hierarchy

Backend — gap on vectors:

  • Semantic/RAG retrieval is scoped by company_id only, not by tier — so tiers are not separate vector knowledge bases yet (SYSTEM_FUNCTIONALITY_MAP.md flags this as MISSING)

Frontend — the mismatch you saw:

  • projects/memory_store.py seeds exactly 3 projects named "Corporate", "Professional", "Personal" — one per tier
  • No POST /projects — users cannot create projects
  • Sidebar shows those three as the project list with sessions underneath (app-shell.tsx, project-list.tsx with Corp/Pro/Me badges)
  • Home page copy literally says "browse projects (Corporate, Professional, Personal)"

So yes — what you saw is exactly what the code produces, and it's far from intended.

Recommended next steps (preserving all G1.5 backend work)

Frontend alignment (your observation is the top priority):

  1. Stop seeding tier-named projects; add user-created projects (POST /projects + "+ New Project" in sidebar)
  2. Move Corporate/Professional/Personal to a Knowledge/Memory area — not the project selector
  3. Sessions stay under projects (that part is already wired)
  4. Render orchestrator → leaders → workers as a tree in the swarm panel (backend already tags role)

Backend follow-ups (no regression to G1.5):

  • Wire /orchestrator/run to build_plan → approve → execute_plan (hierarchical path still only on the new lifecycle endpoints)
  • Add G1.5-specific live E2E tests
  • Optionally tier-scope vector retrieval (deeper memory work)

Why there are so many branches

You have 124 remote refs (122 cursor/* branches plus main). That is not 122 parallel products — it is one phased build executed by Cursor cloud agents, where each phase got its own branch + PR:

phase-0 → phase-1 → … → phase-8z → phase-g15* → phase-f2a-g2-stack
(one branch per agent run, rarely deleted after merge)

Integration happened through land branches (phase-8z-integration-v2, phase-main-merge, phase-f2a-g2-stack) that folded work into main, often via squash/re-implement, so git ancestry does not always show branches as "merged" even when the content is already in main.

Nobody ran branch cleanup. Of ~86 PRs, most are closed (not merged) because work landed via integration branches — but the branches stayed on the remote.

What actually matters (only 3 branches)

BranchStatusAction
cursor/phase-f2a-g2-stack-6750 (PR #86)9 commits ahead of main, 0 behind — clean fast-forwardMerge into main — this is the real tip (F2a–F2d, G1.5k/l, G5, G5a, G2)
cursor/unified-master-plan-v2-6750 (PR #85)1 unique docs commitMerge after #86 — unified master plan v2 (conflicts in docs only)
cursor/dev-environment-setup-dfa7 (PR #84 closed)Only branch with AGENTS.mdYour call — cherry-pick AGENTS.md or drop it

Everything else (119 branches) is either fully merged into main by ancestry, or verified by content check to already exist in main.

Safe consolidation playbook

0. Safety net (do this first)

git fetch --all --prune
git tag backup/pre-consolidation-$(date +%Y%m%d) origin/main
git bundle create ../ii-all-refs-$(date +%Y%m%d).bundle --all

1. Land the integration tip (fast-forward, no conflicts expected)

git checkout main && git pull origin main
git merge --ff-only origin/cursor/phase-f2a-g2-stack-6750
git push origin main
# Or merge PR #86 when ready

2. Fold in unified master plan docs

git merge origin/cursor/unified-master-plan-v2-6750
# Resolve conflicts in docs/UNIFIED_MASTER_PLAN.md, MASTER_PLAN_PROGRESS_AUDIT.md
# Prefer the v2 superset, then: python3 scripts/combine_master_plan.py
git push origin main

3. Optional: restore AGENTS.md

git checkout origin/cursor/dev-environment-setup-dfa7 -- AGENTS.md
git commit -m "chore: restore Cursor Cloud dev env instructions"

4. Delete 119 stale branches (after Steps 1–2 succeed)

# All ancestry-merged branches:
git branch -r --merged origin/main \
| grep 'origin/cursor/' \
| sed 's#origin/##' \
| xargs -n1 git push origin --delete
# Plus 7 verified-stale unmerged branches (content already in main):
for b in phase-8z-integration-v2-6750 docs-blocker-sync-6750 docs-roadmap-status-6750 \
phase-7u-replan-count-persistence-6750 phase-7v-deploy-cutover-6750 \
phase-desktop-prod-test-6750 phase-main-merge-6750; do
git push origin --delete "cursor/$b"
done

5. Verify nothing was lost

# Every remaining cursor/* tip should be an ancestor of main (or intentionally skipped):
git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short)' refs/remotes/origin/cursor/ | while read b; do
git merge-base --is-ancestor "$b" origin/main && echo "OK $b" || echo "ORPHAN $b"
done
# ORPHAN = do NOT delete until merged

i seem to have closed the prs by mistake is that an issue ?

No — closing PRs by mistake is usually not a problem, especially for the ones that mattered.

What closing a PR does and does not do

ActionEffect
Close PRCloses the GitHub review thread only
Does NOTRemove commits from main, delete merged code, or revert branches

Code is only lost if it was never merged/pushed to main and the branch is deleted.

Your important PRs are fine

GitHub currently shows:

PRBranchStatus
#86cursor/phase-f2a-g2-stack-6750MERGED
#85cursor/unified-master-plan-v2-6750MERGED

main is at 7946cbf and includes all of that work (verified: the #86 branch is an ancestor of main).

So even if you clicked “Close” at some point, the code landed on main via the consolidation we ran. You’re not missing F2a–G2, G1.5k/l, G5, G5a, G2, or the unified plan docs.

When closing would matter

Only if you closed a PR whose work never reached main, for example:

  • #84 (dev-environment-setup-dfa7) — CLOSED, not merged → only unique thing is AGENTS.md (still on the branch if not deleted)

Most other CLOSED PRs (#79, #75, #74, etc.) were folded into integration branches and are already in main — closing them is normal cleanup.

If you want to reopen one

On GitHub: Pull requests → Closed → [PR] → Reopen pull request

Or open a new PR from the same branch if it still exists:

git push origin cursor/phase-f2a-g2-stack-6750 # if branch still exists

For #85/#86 you don’t need to — they’re merged and main has everything.

Bottom line: Closing PRs by mistake is a UI/history issue, not a code-loss issue, as long as main has the commits (it does). The only optional follow-up is #84 / AGENTS.md if you still want that file — say if you want that cherry-picked onto main.
